First, we substitute $u=\frac{1}{x}.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\,⟹\,-\text{d}u=\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\text{d}x.
$$

Since $u\to -\infty $ when $x\to {0}^{-}$ and $u\to 0$ when $x\to -\infty ,$ the table for the limits of integration using the rule $u=\frac{1}{x}$ is as follows:

| $x$ | $0$ | $-\infty $ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $-\infty $ | $0$ |

So, the integral in terms of the new variable $u$ is

$$
{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{{e}^{5/x}}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x=-{\int }_{0}^{-\infty }{e}^{5u}\,\text{d}u={\int }_{-\infty }^{0}{e}^{5u}\,\text{d}u.
$$

Now, we proceed by setting the lower bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to -\infty .$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{{e}^{5/x}}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }{\int }_{a}^{0}{e}^{5u}\,\text{d}u \\  & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }{[\frac{{e}^{5u}}{5}]}_{a}^{0} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}{lim}_{a\to -\infty }(1-{e}^{5a}) \\  & =\frac{1}{5}(1-{lim}_{a\to -\infty }{e}^{5a})\end{aligned}
$$

Next, recall the end behavior of the function $y={e}^{5x}$ shown in the graph below:

- ${lim}_{x\to -\infty }{e}^{5x}=0$

- ${lim}_{x\to \infty }{e}^{5x}=\infty $

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14042659/assets/2a24352ca6421b3aa61f3f29e3c19373cca011feafce263775a2f692f67ad36b.png)

Using this to evaluate our integral, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{{e}^{5/x}}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{5}(1-{lim}_{a\to -\infty }{e}^{5a}) \\  & =\frac{1}{5}(1-0) \\  & =\frac{1}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$
